rationale: C10 is the immediately preceding annual Armistice Day proclamation and supplies a concrete template for the child. Both use the same statutory history, move from renewed conflict to rededication to lasting peace, urge the Nation to devote itself anew to promoting permanent peace, and direct officials to display the flag on all public buildings. C02 and C06 share parts of the flag-display machinery, but not the distinctive Armistice Day substance and sequence.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the Congress, by a concurrent resolution of June 4, 1926 ... and, by an act approved May 13, 1938 ... made November 11 of each year a legal holiday ... known as Armistice Day
shared_material.parent_excerpt: the Congress passed a concurrent resolution on June 4, 1926 ... and later provided in an act approved May 13, 1938 ... that the eleventh of November should be a legal holiday and should be celebrated and known as Armistice Day
shared_material.explanation: The same two enactments are recited in the same sequence and for the same operative purpose.

shared_material.child_excerpt: devote themselves anew ... to the task of promoting with fervor and zeal a permanent peace among all the peoples of the earth
shared_material.parent_excerpt: devote themselves anew on that day to the task of promoting a permanent peace among all the people of the earth
shared_material.explanation: This is distinctive, nearly verbatim operative language carried into the later proclamation.

shared_material.child_excerpt: I also direct the appropriate officials of the Government to arrange for the display of the flag of the United States on all public buildings on that day.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I also direct the appropriate officials of the Government to arrange for the display of the flag of the United States on all public buildings on Armistice Day.
shared_material.explanation: The administrative directive is reproduced almost word for word, with only the final temporal reference changed.
